newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia Finmin criticises foreign account costs.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia Finmin criticises foreign account costs.

text.p: Slovenian Finance Minister Mitja Gaspari criticised the high costs of custodian accounts charged by domestic banks to international investors, Slovenian news agency STA said on Tuesday.
"There are enough reasons that the costs of the accounts could be significantly lower," Gaspari said at the start of a four-day financial fair called Kapital in Ljubljana.

Commercial banks, which are due to open the first custodian accounts later this month, said the cost of the accounts would be about 12 percent of the amount handled. Similar accounts in western European countries cost between two and six percent.
"With such policies Slovenian banks will not be able to match foreign competition," Gaspari noted.

The government last year drafted a new law to make it easier for foreign banks to invest in Slovenia by enabling them to open branches. Currently they can only establish subsidiaries, requiring substantial capital outlays.
The law is expected to be passed by parliament later this year.

The Bank of Slovenia in February blocked foreign buying of Slovenian securities, saying internatinal investors must open custodian accounts at one of Slovenia's 14 fully licensed banks in order to be able to trade in Slovenian securities.
Since then the SBI index has dropped by 19.1 percent, while daily volume at an average of 70 million tolars ($0.45 million) is one seventh of its size prior to the ruling.
The banks said the costs would be high due to Bank of Slovenia regulations, whereby banks have to consider money paid into the accounts as liabilities which they must balance against assets.
